text:
Abraham is commanded to take his son, his only son, whom he loves; and of what Abraham feels at the command we are told nothing. The narrator never looks within him. There is no protest, no bargaining, no trace of the man who pleaded with God for Sodom. In place of a character we have a silence, and in that silence lies the whole meaning of the episode. A question is raised there, and it is left unanswered.

The three days of travel may be read as a kind of suspended sentence: outwardly nothing happens, inwardly everything. The narrator lingers on the servants, the wood, the knife, the fire, and so names the instruments of the act before the act itself. Obedience and horror are present together throughout the journey, and neither is ever suffered to prevail over the other. Faith in this story is a geometry, and feeling has no part in it.

Isaac is the child of the covenant, through whom the nations are to be blessed; and the chapter turns that promise into a test, so that, if we set it beside the earlier promise, the difference between the two narrows. Everything in the scene turns upon a single word, _hineni_, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: to God, to Isaac, to the angel. Each time it means something different, and each time it costs him more. To declare himself present is, for Abraham, to consent to loss.

What does Isaac know? We are not told. He carries the wood; he asks about the lamb; he receives an answer that is no answer. Of his thoughts the narrator gives no account, only a verb: they went, both of them, together. The phrase recurs, as though repetition might stand in for explanation, and the question of Isaac's consent is raised and quietly let fall. Obedience, strictly reckoned, leaves nothing over.

A reader who attends to what is missing will be rewarded. Sarah is absent from the chapter entirely, and her death is announced in the very next verse; the scene implies, though it never states, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants, and of Isaac nothing is said. The narrator turns away at precisely the moment where a lesser storyteller would linger. Much of the meaning of the passage depends on these omissions, for a silence of this kind bears witness, and is far from a mere want of matter.

It may be objected that the reticence here reflects only the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains; and in some sense this may be true. Yet elsewhere the narrator tells us plainly what his characters feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence of this chapter is therefore deliberate, and no accident of the form. Restraint, in this narrator, has the force of an accusation against Abraham's God.

The God who promises and the God who demands are left unreconciled; the chapter keeps them side by side and makes no choice between them. Abraham stands on the mountain with the knife raised and the ram not yet seen, and the reader is left standing beside him. The question is past all answering, and its unanswerableness is itself the answer. To read the chapter is to undergo a test of one's own.

Genesis 22 is less a story of sacrifice than a story of reading; we learn from it that the most important things are those a writer declines to say. What Genesis 22 withholds is what it gives, and its brevity is the reader's burden. Abraham's silence, Isaac's question, Sarah's absence, the narrator's refusal to explain: each is a gap, and each gap makes its demand upon us.
